#9788. The Relevance of Software Engineering in Web Applications

Software engineering plays an important role in the development of modern web applications. Today, web applications are used in almost every area of life, including education, banking, communication, healthcare, entertainment, and online shopping.

Developing a successful web application requires more than just writing code. It involves proper planning, designing, testing, security, and maintenance. These activities are part of software engineering.

However, with the introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI), developers can now create applications by simply describing what they want. This practice is commonly known as vibe coding.

Although vibe coding makes development faster and easier, depending entirely on AI without understanding the generated code can create serious problems.

This article discusses the relevance of software engineering in web applications and highlights the dangers of vibe coding and developing WebApps without proper software engineering practices.

Software engineering is the systematic application of engineering principles, methods, and techniques to the development, testing, operation, and maintenance of software.

It is not just about writing code. It involves several stages:

For example, when developing an online shopping application, developers must plan how customers will register, log in, search for products, make payments, and track their orders.

Without proper planning, the application may contain errors and security problems.

Software engineering is important in WebApps for several reasons.

Web applications often store personal information such as names, passwords, addresses, and payment details. Software engineering helps developers protect this information against unauthorized access and cyberattacks.

A good web application should perform its functions correctly. Software engineering encourages proper testing to identify and correct errors before the application is released.

Web applications need regular updates and improvements. Properly organized code makes it easier for developers to correct errors and add new features.

Scalability is the ability of an application to handle an increasing number of users. Proper software design helps an application grow without constantly failing.

Planning and testing help developers identify problems early. This reduces the cost of correcting errors after an application has been released.

Software engineering helps developers create applications that are easy to use, responsive, accessible, and efficient.

Vibe coding is a modern approach to software development where a person uses ordinary language to describe an application and depends on Artificial Intelligence tools to generate much of the code.

For example, a person may tell an AI tool:

"Create an online shopping website where customers can register, buy products, and make payments."

The AI tool may generate HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and other parts of the application.

Vibe coding can help beginners learn programming, build prototypes, and complete simple tasks faster.

However, problems arise when developers accept AI-generated code without understanding, reviewing, or testing it.

Although vibe coding has advantages, it also has several disadvantages.

AI-generated code may contain security weaknesses. For example, a login system may fail to protect user accounts properly or may allow unauthorized users to access restricted pages.

AI can generate code that works but is poorly organized. It may contain repeated code, unnecessary functions, and complicated structures.

Some developers assume that an application is ready simply because it opens successfully. However, the application may still contain errors that appear when users interact with it.

AI-generated applications may have poorly designed databases. This can cause duplicated information, incorrect relationships, and difficulties managing records.

Developers who depend entirely on AI may fail to develop their programming and problem-solving skills. They may struggle to identify and correct errors without AI assistance.

Sharing passwords, API keys, or private customer information with unapproved AI tools can expose sensitive information.

When developers do not understand the code generated by AI, updating and improving the application can become difficult.

An application may look professional because it has attractive colours, buttons, and dashboards. However, its appearance does not guarantee that it is secure, reliable, or functional.

Developing web applications without following proper software engineering practices can lead to serious problems.

These problems show that developing a WebApp is not just about making it attractive. It must also be secure, reliable, and functional.

Developers can reduce these risks by following proper software engineering practices.

1. Requirement Analysis: Developers should understand what the application is expected to do before development begins.

2. System Design: Developers should plan the structure of the application, database, and relationships between different components.

3. Proper Coding: Developers should write clean, organized, reusable, and understandable code.

4. Software Testing: Applications should be tested to identify errors and confirm that their features work correctly.

5. Database Security: Developers should protect stored information through appropriate access controls and secure database practices.

6. Code Review: Code should be reviewed to identify errors and security weaknesses.

7. Regular Maintenance: Applications should receive regular updates, corrections, and security improvements.

8. Responsible Use of AI: AI should be used as an assistant rather than a replacement for programming knowledge and software engineering practices.

Artificial Intelligence is changing the way software is developed. AI tools help developers generate code, understand programming concepts, and complete tasks faster.

However, AI does not remove the need for software engineering.

Developers must still understand, review, test, and improve the code generated by AI.

For example, AI can generate a registration form, but the developer must ensure that user information is validated, passwords are properly protected, and the database stores information correctly.

The best approach is to combine AI tools with software engineering principles.

Software engineering is an essential part of developing successful web applications. It helps ensure that applications are properly planned, designed, developed, tested, secured, and maintained.

A professional web application should not be judged only by its appearance or how quickly it was developed. Its quality should also be measured by its security, reliability, performance, and ability to meet users' needs.

Therefore, developers should not abandon software engineering because of Artificial Intelligence. Instead, they should use AI alongside proper engineering practices.

The future of web development should not only be about generating code quickly, but about building applications that are secure, reliable, useful, and sustainable.

#9787. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9786. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:

With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:

CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:

The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

You can also train on a cloud GPU with Hugging Face Jobs. Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

#9785. Extra Eyes on the Line

On most production lines, a camera can see every part, most parts are fine, and the expensive thing is a trained inspector's attention. Inspectors don't need a replacement. They need an extra set of eyes.

So I built LineSight, a demo that takes a photo or a short video clip of a manufactured part and returns three things: a PASS / REVIEW / FAIL recommendation, the visible defects with severity and location, and the most relevant entries from a library of inspection guidance. A human inspector always makes the final call. The AI's job is to focus their attention.

The constraint I gave myself: the whole stack had to have zero idle cost. No always-on servers, no managed vector database burning money overnight. Everything bills per request or not at all.

This isn't my first time pointing code at images. Years ago I worked at HP, which owned the online photo service Snapfish at the time. I was brought onto a team building image processing technologies. We started with open source libraries like OpenCV: looking at images, running interesting conversions, and pulling individual frames out of video to examine them. Then came detection: finding a face in an image, or finding the area of interest and cropping to it.

The hard part was never the code. It was the training data. To teach an algorithm what a face is, I had to break "face" down into the features that make one: eyes, eyebrows, a nose, a mouth, and where they sit relative to each other. Then I had to feed it about 100,000 sample images, some with faces and some without, so it could learn which patterns meant "face" and which were just shadows or background. Every miss meant more samples and another training run.

That toolkit is all over manufacturing, for good reason. OpenCV is fast, free to run, and deterministic. It can find a part on a conveyor, confirm a label is where it belongs, measure a hole, or flag a frame that differs from a known-good reference.

Where it struggles is judgment. A classical detector answers the question you tuned it for. Ask whether a mark is a scratch or a reflection, how bad it is, or what the inspector should do about it, and you're building a new model or a new pile of thresholds. Every new part, defect type, or lighting change means more tuning.

That's what changed most for me. Face detection took 100,000 images. LineSight was never shown a single training image. What it knows about these parts comes from a prompt and about 20 text records in the reference library. When the bike frame came in, there was no weld detector to build or retrain. The model judged the welds on its own, and the low similarity score showed the library had nothing to back it up.

So this isn't one replacing the other. LineSight still uses OpenCV to pull frames from video. The old toolkit does the fast, mechanical work, and the model does the part that used to need a person.

The full source (CDK stack, runtime, Streamlit app, and the synthetic reference library) is on GitHub: scooteronce/linesight-quality-inspection

The classic failure mode of LLM pipelines is parsing. The model wraps its JSON in prose, or invents an enum value, and your pipeline falls over at 2 a.m.

The Claude API's structured outputs feature eliminates the whole category. You attach a JSON schema to the request, and the response is guaranteed to conform: valid JSON, correct types, enums enforced.

The schema constrains inspection_status to PASS | REVIEW | FAIL, severities to low | medium | high, and requires evidence and a location for every defect. There is no JSON parsing code in the project beyond json.loads. No regex, no "find the first brace," no retry-on-malformed loop.

A related prompt-design point: the system is deliberately asymmetric. The prompt instructs the model to use FAIL only for clearly visible material defects, and REVIEW whenever the image is blurry, obstructed, or ambiguous. In quality inspection a false PASS is the expensive failure, so uncertainty routes to a human by design.

The same rule applies to failures. If the model declines to analyze an image, the runtime returns REVIEW with low confidence instead of an error, so the part still lands in front of a person.

The retrieval layer matches each finding against a library of reference records: defect examples ("deep groove with substrate exposure is high severity; hold for review") and process guidance ("reflections can resemble scratches; use diffuse lighting").

The standard recipe is OpenSearch Serverless, and that's where the zero-idle-cost constraint bites. OpenSearch Serverless bills for minimum capacity continuously, roughly $175+/month whether you query it or not. For a reference library of a few dozen records, that's absurd.

Instead, embeddings are precomputed once at build time and shipped inside the runtime bundle as a JSON file. At inspection time, the runtime embeds only the model's one-sentence defect description (a Titan call costing a few millionths of a dollar) and ranks the library in-process:

Pure Python, no numpy, no index, no network hop. For ~20 records of 1,024 dimensions this runs in milliseconds.

It's also honest about its limits. When I fed the system a photo of a badly welded bike frame, the top reference came back at 0.338 similarity. The library has no welding records, and the low score says so instead of pretending. When a real defect library outgrows this, the upgrade path is a managed store. That's a scale decision, not a starting requirement.

Claude doesn't ingest video directly, but it doesn't need to. The app extracts evenly spaced frames from an uploaded clip (OpenCV, sampling segment midpoints so the first and last moments are represented), resizes them, and sends them as one batch.

The runtime interleaves a "Frame N:" label before each image and extends the prompt: report each distinct defect once, name the frame where it's most visible, and use agreement across frames as evidence. A mark visible from several angles is stronger evidence than something that appears in exactly one frame, which is probably glare.

That last instruction matters. Multi-frame input isn't just "more pictures." It gives the model a cheap consistency check that a single photo can't provide. The schema gains a required frame field per defect, so the UI can show the inspector exactly which sampled frame to look at.

Cost scales with frames sampled, not clip length: an 8-frame inspection costs roughly 8x a single image.

In the review app you pick 2 to 12 frames per clip. The runtime accepts up to 20 frames and 5 MB per request, and the app lowers JPEG quality until the batch fits.

The runtime calls Claude through the official Anthropic SDK's Bedrock client rather than hand-rolling boto3 request bodies. You get the Messages API surface, typed errors, and features like structured outputs with no translation layer:

Here's the gotcha that cost me a debugging session: this endpoint does not authorize against the classic bedrock:InvokeModel action. The runtime's first invocation failed with a 403 naming an action I'd never granted:

The fix is one extra IAM statement alongside your usual Bedrock grants:

I scoped the model grants with a wildcard (anthropic.claude-* foundation models plus the us.anthropic.claude-* cross-region inference profiles), so swapping models is an environment-variable change, not an IAM change.

That matters for cost tuning. Switching VISION_MODEL_ID to Claude Haiku 5.5 makes each inspection about 40x cheaper per token (on prompts under 100K tokens, which an inspection always is). For a bounded task with a fixed schema, that's worth A/B testing against your own parts.

Deploy it, use it twice a week, and the bill is two inspections.

New AWS accounts come with free-tier credits that cover thousands of inspections.

The honest caveat: this cost profile is a property of demo-scale choices. A production system reintroduces always-on baseline: a managed vector store once the reference library grows, a hosted authenticated review app instead of local Streamlit, VPC networking, image and audit-trail storage. The inspection workflow and the Bedrock calls stay identical. It's the infrastructure around them that starts the meter.

The repo inspects one upload at a time. Here's how I'd point the same pieces at a line's output. This part is a design, not something the repo does yet.

At about a cent per single-image inspection on Opus 5.5, 1,000 parts a shift is roughly $10. An 8-frame burst multiplies that by about 8. If that's too much, there are two levers: inspect a sample instead of every part, or switch to Haiku 5.5. Test both against your own parts before trusting either.

Latency is the other limit. At 8 to 11 seconds per inspection, this works for sampled audits and end-of-line holds. It's too slow to gate a fast line part by part, and that's where classical CV still wins.

Idle cost is zero, but delete the stack when you're finished so no IAM roles or runtimes linger in your account:

That removes the AgentCore runtime and its role. No images are stored, so there's nothing else to empty. Leave the CDK bootstrap resources alone unless nothing else in the account uses them.

If you're putting vision models to work on the factory floor, I'd like to hear how you handle the human-review handoff. Drop a comment, or follow for more posts on AWS and applied AI.

#9782. I ran 42 more agent sprints on a harder task. Here's what the workflow didn't fix.

In the first post a Scrum workflow for coding agents looked clean: with the skill, 6 of 6 runs met every item of the Definition of Done, against 3 of 6 without it. Several of you pointed out the obvious catch. One small task, one model, three runs per side. That's a hint, not a result.

So I ran a bigger one, and I wrote down the rules before I looked at a single run.

Two runs per cell first. The pre-registered rule then flagged every model as inconsistent, so every cell got a third run. 42 runs, 14 hours, all on subscriptions.

It makes the process complete. Without it, review verdicts and the sprint reports were missing in 10 of 21 runs. With it, 2 and 1 of 21. Same pattern as last time, now across seven models instead of one.

It also made runs cheaper for Sonnet, Opus, gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6-astra. I expected the opposite.

And nobody, in either arm, committed the generator's write into the other module. Strong models respect write regions when you spell them out.

It doesn't reliably make the code more correct. Hidden tests went up for Haiku (+1.3 of 4 items), Sonnet and gpt-5.6-sol. They stayed flat for gpt-6.1-sol and Astra, and dipped slightly for Opus and Luna. The whole hidden suite passed in 3 of 21 runs without the skill and 4 of 21 with it. A workflow can make sure tests exist and get reviewed. It can't make the reviewer spot an authorization rule nobody wrote down.

It doesn't help every small model. Haiku gained the most. Luna, the small Codex model, got worse with the skill. One of its runs merged nothing at all.

It can get expensive. With gpt-5.6-sol, the skill's portable mode burned through tokens: one attempt alone read 17.9 million input tokens. Cost per passed hidden item went from $0.72 to $2.79.

This one stung. One Definition-of-Done item checks that implementation and tests were committed separately for each item. My grader found an item's commits through its branch or an item ID in the commit message. Lanewright deletes item branches after merging, and its role commits don't repeat the ID. So the grader saw only the docs commits and failed that item in 17 of 21 runs with the skill.

The separation was there. Reading the same commits from each merged pull request, with the same rules, gives 19 of 21 with the skill and 21 of 21 without.

I didn't touch the frozen grader. The report shows its numbers as the main result and the re-scored ones next to them. With the fix, the skill raised the Definition-of-Done score in 6 of 7 models. Without it, in 3. You can decide which one you believe; both are in the data.

Matched by list price, the Claude model met as many or more items in 7 of 8 comparisons. Codex was cheaper per passed item on the cheap and middle pairs. On the expensive pairs it flipped. Price isn't ability and the model generations differ, so I'd read this as a sketch, not a ranking.

Sixteen more runs start this weekend: Lanewright against the free scrum-kit in Claude Code, across four model settings, including a cheap orchestrator driving stronger roles. After that the task, hidden tests and harness go public too.

Everything above, with every run's numbers, the pre-registration and the deviations log, is here: bench/hard-2026-11-10.

Lanewright is a paid skill on Agensi: Lanewright on Agensi. Version 1.0.1, the exact build tested here.

The planning side is free. Four MIT skills take a loose brief to an SRS, a weekly sprint plan and a backlog a human signs off before any agent starts: Intake, SRS, Sprint Planner, Backlog Check.

And scrum-kit stays free and MIT, with prompts in Bahasa Indonesia.

#9781. BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)

We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.

BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)

Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):

It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

[1] Yu, Qiying, et al. "DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025): 113222–113244.

#9780. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

#9779. Replay-Safe Verification with PostgreSQL

Email verification looks simple until a request times out at the worst possible moment. The API may have stored a token, queued a message, and then lost the connection before returning 201 Created. The client retries because it cannot tell whether the operation failed or only the response was lost.

That retry is not a new intent; its a new delivery attempt. A useful backend design makes both attempts converge on one verification workflow. The result is fewer duplicate messages, fewer invalidated tokens, and a much clearer support trail.

This pattern is also valuable in test environments. A disposable email inbox, for example, should be tied to one logical verification run instead of being recreated every time a worker sees a transient error. The same data boundary that protects production users makes automated tests easier to reason about.

The idempotency key represents the logical signup operation, not the individual network attempt. If the server receives this request twice with the same tenant, key, and payload, it should return the same logical result. It should not mint a second token merely because the first HTTP response was hiden by a timeout.

The key needs a scope. At minimum, include the tenant or user identity in the lookup. A global key such as signup-123 can collide across customers, while a key scoped only to the email address can accidentally merge two intentional verification flows.

Validate the request before creating any side effect. Normalize the email for comparison, reject an invalid key, and calculate a request fingerprint from the fields that define the operation. Store the fingerprint with the idempotency record.

A repeated key with the same fingerprint can return the stored response. A repeated key with a different fingerprint should produce 409 Conflict. Quietly changing the meaning of an existing key creates an incident that is difficult to reconstruct later.

The record should preserve enough response data to replay the result:

Do not store a raw verification token in a general-purpose idempotency table. Keep secrets in the verification record, preferably as a digest, and make the replay response contain only the fields the client originally received.

Treat the verification process as a small state machine instead of a boolean that workers update from memory. A practical set of states is:

created -> send_pending -> sent -> verified

with explicit failure and expiry paths such as send_failed and expired.

Each transition should record who or what caused it, when it happened, and the provider message ID if one exists. The transition table are the durable boundary between an API request and an asynchronous worker. If a worker crashes after the provider accepts a message, the next worker can inspect the state rather than blindly sending again.

Keep transitions monotonic where possible. A late send_failed event must not move an already verified address backwards. If a business rule allows a new verification after expiry, create a new attempt ID instead of reusing the old row.

Application checks such as SELECT ...; if no row, INSERT ... are not enough under concurrent requests. Two API instances can both observe the gap and both insert a record. Let PostgreSQL enforce the invariant:

Use a transaction for the idempotency insert and the verification row creation. On a unique violation, fetch the existing row and compare its request fingerprint. Matching fingerprints take the replay path. Mismatches return 409; they should never be silently overwritten.

For the worker, claim work with a lease or FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. A lease gives a crashed worker time to recover without allowing two workers to send forever at the same time. It does not make an external email provider transactional, so the provider message ID and an attempt number should be recorded whenever available.

The worker should follow a narrow sequence:

If the process dies between steps 3 and 4, the next run faces an ambiguity: the message may have been sent. That is why a reconciliation job matters. Search provider events by the stable attempt ID, then mark the database from evidence. Sending immediately again may create a duplicate; waiting forever may leave a user stuck.

The same approach makes test runs more useful. A run receipt for disposable email tests can record the attempt ID, expected subject, observed message ID, and cleanup status. Small evidence like this is often more usefull than a long CI log.

Log the tenant-safe verification ID, idempotency key hash, attempt number, state transition, and correlation ID. Avoid logging the token or complete email content. Metrics should separate duplicate requests, provider failures, lease expirations, and reconciliation outcomes.

In practise, these signals make a timeout incident much less mysterious. The question changes from “why did the user get two emails?” to “which attempt crossed the provider boundary without a committed transition?”

The goal is not to pretend that distributed systems never retry. The goal is to make a retry ordinary: one logical verification, one durable state history, and a response that can be replayed safely.

#9778. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas ProWritingAid offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.
  • Grammarly provides Android and IOS apps whereas ProWritingAid doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.
  • Grammarly offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas ProWritingAid  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.
  • Grammarly is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas ProWritingAid is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.
  • Grammarly finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas ProWritingAid identifies run-on sentences and fragments.
  • Grammarly provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. ProWritingAid’s support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.
  • Grammarly offers many features in its free plan, whereas ProWritingAid offers some basic features in the free plan.
  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • ProWritingAid comes with three pricing structures. The full-year cost of ProWritingAid is $79, while its lifetime plans cost $339. You also can opt for a monthly plan of $20.
  • Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly and $12/month for an annual subscription.
  • The Business plan costs $12.50 per month for each member of your company.

ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons

Grammarly Pros

  • It allows you to fix common mistakes like grammar and spelling.
  • Offers most features in the free plan
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Proofread your writing and correct all punctuation, grammar, and spelling errors.
  • Allows you to make changes to a document without altering its formatting.
  • Helps users improve vocabulary
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.
  • Enhance the readability of your sentence
  • Free mobile apps 
  • Offers  free version

Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in a premium plan
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy
  • The free version is ideal for basic spelling and grammatical mistakes, but it does not correct advanced writing issues.
  • Some features are not available for Mac.

ProwritingAid Pros

  • It offers more than 20 different reports to help you improve your writing.
  • Less expensive than other grammar checkers.
  • This tool helps you strengthen your writing style as it offers big-picture feedback.
  • ProWritingAid has a life plan with no further payments required.
  • Compatible with Google Docs!
  • Prowritingaid works on both Windows and Mac.
  • They offer more integrations than most tools.

ProWritingAid Cons

  • Editing can be a little more time-consuming when you add larger passages of text.
  • ProWritingAid currently offers no mobile app for Android or iOS devices.
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in premium plans.
  • All recommendations are not accurate

Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

  • For example, go for Grammarly  if you are a non-fiction writer
  • Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.
  • ProWritingAid is better at catching errors found in long-form content. However, Grammarly is more suited to short blog posts and other similar tasks.
  • ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.
