#9775. The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:

This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

If you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso

We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object

The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

We then follow these steps within the training loop:

The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:

In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

Gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

Thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗

Singapore, Singapore, November 12th, 2026/Chainwire/--The AVA Foundation and Travala, the Binance-backed crypto travel booking platform, today announced AVA 3.0, accompanied by a roadmap that reinforces AVA token utility on Travala.

As the AVA token’s primary commercial application, Travala is the focus of the new plan, which builds on AVA 2.0 and emphasises real-world travel products, transparent buybacks, and measurable member value.

AVA 3.0 leads with existing products. The AVA Smart Program has more than 180,000 members, who lock AVA to save up to 13% on travel and receive other perks. Members can also pay for discounted travel with AVA and receive AVA rewards through the Travala AI Agent, which is live on BNB Chain in collaboration with Binance Pay.

Backing the program is a monthly buyback. Each month, the AVA Foundation buys back AVA to replenish member giveback rewards, and Travala matches it and locks its share in the AVA Strategic Reserve. The AVA Buyback Multiplier scales Travala’s match between 1x and 3x as AVA givebacks grow, with a total monthly buyback potential of up to 4x AVA givebacks. More bookings generate more givebacks, and more givebacks mean bigger buybacks.

To date, 5,604,414 AVA has been bought back by the Foundation, with 779,691.92 AVA (representing 1.1% of circulating supply) permanently locked in Travala’s AVA Strategic Reserve. 17.5% of AVA’s circulating supply is locked as the ecosystem targets a long-term goal of 30%.

Two launches are next. Increased AVA lock levels for new Smart members are expected in November, while existing members keep their current locks and can use the new Smart Boost feature to increase their AVA locks and potential rewards. AVA+ Partners follows, with the launch expected in Q1 2027. It will allow partner projects to lock AVA for their tokens to be accepted as payment on Travala.

The Foundation is exploring several further ideas for 2027 and beyond, including AI booking agents that recognise Smart membership tiers to apply membership benefits, curated travel specials available exclusively in AVA, and VIP travel concierge access based on AVA holdings.

“Through every market since we started, one thing has held true: AVA is at its best when it's used,” said Juan Otero, Travala CEO and co-founder, and Steven Hipwell, Travala co-founder and AVA Foundation Lead Contributor. “AVA 3.0 isn’t about grand promises; it’s about evolving what already works.”

The AVA token and all existing memberships, locks, and rewards continue as normal. Partnerships beyond Travala will be assessed where they deliver clear commercial value.

#9772. Building an AI App to Strengthen Human Thinking: How We Used SurrealDB Agent Memory

Students who build with AI tools often end up with code that works and ideas behind it they can't explain. A tool that forgets every session can't tell them whether that is changing. It can't say they needed less help today, or that their guess about what they could explain was closer than last time.

Lumente fosters questioning and curiosity in programming students who build with AI, through learning the concepts behind their own code. A student picks a concept like JWT and works it out by asking questions, and a map of four parts (category, similar concepts and differences, defining features and classification) shows them where to look. Our Claude agents ask the questions at first, then the help fades and the student starts asking, because that's the skill we want them to build.

Lumente's own database already kept each student's levels for the code that sets the scores. What its agents were missing was memory. The hint giver answers when a student taps Help, and the coach writes a note at the end of each session, but neither could mention an earlier session. This post is how we gave those two agents long-term memory with SurrealDB Agent Memory, without storing anything students wrote. Now they can tell a student how this session compares with the last one, and the app shows the exact fact behind each thing they say.

You can find our repository, demo video and live app here.

For the coach to say "your guess was closer than last time", it has to remember last time. SurrealDB Agent Memory gave us that, and it let us write each fact ourselves, so it stores our sentences exactly as we wrote them and doesn't run a model on them.

It also links each new value to the old one, keeps the history, and can forget a whole scope in one call, so we didn't have to build any of that. It went live in our production app on Oct 23 and is still on.

We started from one rule: nothing a student types goes into memory. Their answers and questions are kept in Lumente's own database, never in Agent Memory. Memory only gets short sentences our code writes from numbers the app has already worked out, like "Last time on JWT you guessed 4 and proved 2."

Memory doesn't know who the student is, either. Each student's facts live in their own scope, learner/, and the pseudonym is a salted hash of their sign-in ID, so memory never sees a name or email.

And students stay in control of it. The Memory sheet in the app shows them what Lumente remembers about them and how it changed. Delete my data calls POST /scopes/forget, which removes their whole scope in one call, and when we checked the live service afterward, there was nothing left to read.

Lumente's architecture, with Agent Memory beside the code that sets scores

We write each fact as one sentence from a template. There are three kinds:

Each fact is one triple: the entity is the student's concept (topic/_), the key says what the fact is about, and the value is the sentence.

We send it with infer: "triples". By default, POST /facts uses infer: "full", where a model reads the text you send and extracts entities, attributes and relations from it. With "triples", we hand Agent Memory the structured triple ourselves, and it stores it as given. Our code already knows each fact exactly, so extraction could only add time, cost and the chance of a wrong fact.

The labels carry the numbers, plus the session, the turn and the agent whose work the fact records, and they came back exactly the way we sent them. Each fact goes out in its own request:

api/src/memory.ts L243-245 and L504-513, with the error handling taken out.

This is the request behind the gap fact the coach cites below, without the pseudonym and session ID:

When a student's level on a part changes, we write the same key again, and this is where long-term memory earns its place. Agent Memory sets supersedes on the new row and closes the old one with validUntil by itself, and our code doesn't touch either. SurrealDB's docs call this "closed in time, not erased."

So Lumente always reads the current level, and the history of how the student got there stays readable. The Memory sheet shows students that history. Next to each level, it shows how many agent calls received that fact, which we count from our own logs.

The Memory sheet before and after a JWT session. On the left: the last result and the one before it. On the right: the new result superseded the last one, which stays in the history, and the read counts went from 1 to 3.

Agent Memory has one route that returns an entity's full history. When we measured it on the live service, it took 290 to 370 ms, well inside our 1.5-second budget. Before the hint giver or the coach runs, the API calls that route, keeps the newest value of each key, and skips any rows from the current session.

Each agent gets at most 8 facts: the current level of each part, then the latest gap, then the parts that took the most Help. The hint giver and the coach read the same scope, so a hint can use a level that the evaluator's verdicts set.

api/src/memory.ts L332-342. The history read is GET /entities/topic/{name}/history (L247-265).

A remark like "your guess was closer than last time" only helps if the student can trust it. Every row in Agent Memory has its own ID, so a citation can point at one exact fact. We put each fact in the prompt as one line with its ID, and the prompt tells the agent to use only those facts and to list the IDs it used in cites.

This is the coach's exchange from one of our JWT sessions:

Claude could still make up an ID we never sent, so the API checks every hint and coach reply with verifyCites. It keeps only the IDs we sent and logs the rest, which means a made-up source never shows up on screen. We have a test where the hint giver cites a fake ID, and only the real one reaches the student.

The student sees each fact we kept under the message, after "From what Lumente remembers:". "Bigger group" is what we call the part that the app shows as "Category".

Left: a hint citing row a9f8jkmhssc13sdy8eze. Right: the coach citing row kdjcdbq1pq1mbg9du2si, in a session with a guess of 5 and a score of 6.

Memory can't change a score, because the code that sets the scores never sees it. advance() is plain code with no model in it, and it decides what happens next and sets every level and point. Our six Claude agents judge what the answers mean and write the words.

The API hands advance() a wrapped callAgent. The wrapper adds the facts to the hint giver's and the coach's input and leaves every other call alone, and advance() only carries the verified IDs onto the message.

api/src/memory.ts L554-567, used at api/src/app.ts L325-326.

The evaluator, whose verdicts feed the score, never gets memory, so a wrong, old or deleted fact can't change a number. Sessions and scores stay in SurrealDB Cloud, separate from Agent Memory.

If memory is slow, empty or turned off, the two agents get the same input they had before we added memory, without a block, and the session keeps going. Their instructions tell them to use only the facts in and never to make up an earlier session.

Three details are worth planning for if you build on Agent Memory. We first saw them on Oct 23 and our code handles all three, and the service may have changed since.

At Build North 2026, Lumente placed in the top 10 of more than 50 teams and was runner-up for Best Use of SurrealDB Agent Memory.

We also asked a few people to try it, most of them developers. Several told us the same thing: when they broke down a concept they thought they knew, they hit a wall, and realized they had never asked themselves what the concept itself was. One student put it this way:

"I thought I knew the concept well enough to explain it. [...] When I started breaking it down, I got to see the fundamentals that were usually overlooked. [...] It made me question: what do I actually know? And how well do I actually know it?"

Next is Check the AI. Today Lumente practices questioning, interpretation, analysis, explanation and self-examination, on concepts: figuring an idea out, telling it apart from similar ones, explaining it in your own words, and checking your prediction against what you proved. Check the AI adds evaluation and inference, practiced on what an AI tells you: judging whether its answer holds up and what follows from it. Questioning stays underneath both. We'll start it once learners show they improve on the concepts.

Memory matters even more there. Judging what an AI tells you is a skill that grows over many sessions, never in one. Without memory, each session starts from zero and that growth stays invisible, to the student and to us. With it, Lumente can show a student, fact by fact, how their judgment of AI is getting sharper.

You can find the memory code in api/src/memory.ts and the contract in agents/CONTRACTS.md.

#9771. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9770. SkyW4lker Exposed: A Growing Microsoft 365 Phishing Threat to American Enterprises

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

Online interactive sandbox for DFIR/SOC investigations. Fast malware analysis and cybersecurity threat detection.

SkyW4lker (SkyW4lker x365 Sentinel) is an active device-code phishing kit targeting Microsoft 365 users in the United States, Europe, and other regions. By abusing Microsoft’s legitimate authentication process, the kit can give attackers access to corporate accounts without stealing passwords or bypassing MFA. This puts business emails, sensitive documents, and other Microsoft 365 resources at risk of unauthorized access.

The ANY.RUN team identified 618 sandbox analyses related to SkyW4lker between June and October 21, 2026, with 46% of submissions coming from the United States. Activity increased from 20 analyses in June to 200 in September, highlighting the growing exposure of organizations relying on Microsoft 365.

JavaScript obfuscation (obfuscator.io), Device-Code phishing, Geolocation detection, IP-address detection, CAPTCHA verification

Email attachments (.pdf, .docx, .xls/xlsx and others), redirection links and lure pages (including Google Maps, Google Images, Miro, Zoom and others)

URL patterns: /session_public.php?action= /endpoints/confirm_visit.php /js/url_helper.js /js/endpoint.js /js/client_geo.js

The United States accounts for 47% of SkyW4lker-related sandbox submissions, more than twice the share of any other country. With the campaign exploiting legitimate Microsoft authentication processes and routine business communications, these findings raise concerns for US enterprises about how effectively existing security controls can identify suspicious activity before it leads to account compromise.

SkyW4lker highlights several security risks that organizations need to account for when protecting business-critical systems and employee identities:

Stop account compromise before it disrupts your business.Detect threats earlier and reduce response costs.

You can examine the full SkyW4lker attack chain in this ANY.RUN Sandbox analysis.

The attacker sends the victim a phishing email with a password-protected attachment. Typical subjects involve commercial offers, contracts, invoices, or confidential documents. The attachment is a PDF, DOCX, or XLSX file, and the password is provided in the email body.

The document contains a link to a CAPTCHA page. Some variants include an additional lure page hosted on a legitimate service such as Miro, Google Sites, or Zoom, which redirects the victim to the next step.

Finally, the victim is directed to a phishing page that instructs them to enter a device code on Microsoft’s legitimate authentication page, potentially granting the attacker access to their Microsoft 365 account.

The phishing page relies on obfuscated JavaScript functions and separate script files. Using ANY.RUN’s In-Browser Data Inspection, analysts can examine the page’s DOM and HTTP activity to understand how these scripts operate.

The scripts keep the page in regular contact with the PHP backend and determine the location of the victim from their IP address. Within the page DOM, the main script loads additional modules, sets click handlers on buttons and builds GET requests to the PHP endpoint /session_public.php with the action parameter (start or poll).

With action=start, the script sends the geolocation and IP address of the victim and receives a session ID. After that, it sends a request with action=poll every few seconds to check whether the victim has authenticated.

The other modules of the phishing page are listed below:

Determines the location of the victim from the response of one of three services: ip-api[.]com, ipapi[.]co or ipwho[.]is. The location can also be obtained through the PHP endpoint php/endpoints/client_geo.php.

Base script with helper wrappers for URL handling, such as building GET parameters and appending slashes.

Tracks the state of the victim. It logs the e-mail address, password, browser, MFA status, country and other auxiliary fields used during authentication and sends them to the PHP backend at php/endpoints/accounts.php.

A single phishing URL can be the starting point for uncovering an entire campaign. In the SkyW4lker investigation, identifying the malicious page was only the beginning. Analysts needed to trace related activity, identify additional infrastructure, and determine how far the campaign extended. Traditionally, connecting these findings requires repeated IOC lookups, manual correlation, and searching through previous investigations.

ANY.RUN’s major new upgrade, Related Threat Context, makes this process significantly faster and easier. By bringing connections to previous sandbox investigations and threat intelligence directly into the Interactive Sandbox, it helps analysts discover related threats, reuse existing findings, and expand investigations with fewer manual steps.

With more than 700,000 security professionals and 16,000 organizations worldwide using ANY.RUN, analysts can draw on a vast pool of real-world investigation data to uncover connections that might otherwise take considerably longer to find.

During our SkyW4lker investigation, the new Related analyses section surfaced previous sandbox sessions sharing the same URL patterns. This gave analysts an immediate starting point for tracing related activity instead of manually searching for connections across individual investigations.

Using the distinctive PHP endpoint /session_public.php, we moved into ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence Lookup in a single click, discovered additional phishing activity, and expanded the campaign cluster.

The investigation demonstrates the practical value of Related Threat Context: less time spent searching for connections, faster discovery of related infrastructure, and more evidence available to guide the next investigation step.

The same approach can be applied to other suspicious URLs and indicators, allowing SOC teams to build on previous investigations and uncover related threat infrastructure faster.

Tier 1 analysts spend less time on repetitive IOC research, gaining more evidence to support accurate triage and escalation decisions. Tier 2 analysts receive richer investigation context, helping them focus on cases that genuinely require deeper analysis.

By connecting individual alerts to existing threat intelligence, Related Threat Context helps SOC teams shorten investigation cycles, reduce unnecessary manual work, and make better-informed response decisions.

Give your SOC the context they need for faster triage.Cut repetitive investigations. Increase Tier 1 productivity.

Each phishing page has its own backend, so the administration panel is likely to be hosted on the same domain. Further analysis of the Threat Intelligence Lookup results and data from other sources revealed an administration panel at /admin/index.php.

The CSS styles (command-center.css) suggest the following capabilities of the kit:

Further investigation revealed another important finding: SkyW4lker shares several technical components with Gabagool, a credential phishing kit.

A search in ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence for the unique module paths of SkyW4lker url:”/js/client_geo.js” or url:”/js/url_helper.js” or url:”/js/endpoint.js”) also returns sandbox sessions tagged gabagool. Gabagool was first observed on 23 April 2026, two months before SkyW4lker, and has used the endpoint.js and url_helper.js modules since late April and early May. The two kits share several other features:

client_geo.js, url_helper.js, endpoint.js (since July 2026)

client_geo.js, url_helper.js, endpoint.js (since late April 2026)

We therefore assess with high confidence that Gabagool and SkyW4lker are built by the same developer. Gabagool harvests logins and passwords through accounts.php, whereas SkyW4lker abuses the device-code flow through session_public.php, so we regard them as two attack modes of one platform. The identical directories on shared hosts may also point to a common operator; however, the available data does not allow us to distinguish one operator from several customers of the same platform.

The SkyW4lker investigation reveals several technical indicators and attack patterns that security teams can use to identify related phishing activity. For organizations, these findings also highlight opportunities to strengthen identity security and reduce the impact of potential account compromise.

Hunt for SkyW4lker’s technical fingerprints. Look for requests to /session_public.php?action=start and repeated /session_public.php?action=poll calls. Check the JavaScript modules and URL patterns identified in this research to uncover related infrastructure.

Connect phishing activity with suspicious sign-ins. Monitor Microsoft Entra ID logs for unexpected device-code authentication, particularly following suspicious emails or document-sharing requests. Correlating authentication events with phishing indicators can help identify potential account compromise.

Expand investigations beyond individual IOCs. ANY.RUN’s newly introduced Related Threat Context puts connected sandbox analyses at analysts’ fingertips, with a one-click pivot to threat intelligence context for deeper threat hunting. In the SkyW4lker investigation, this helped expand the campaign cluster, while further analysis revealed shared infrastructure and code similarities with Gabagool.

Investigate potential follow-on activity. When account compromise is suspected, review subsequent Microsoft 365 activity to identify affected resources, unauthorized access, and possible attempts to target other users.

Give Tier 1 the evidence to make faster decisions.Keep more cases at Tier 1 with 30% fewer escalations.

SkyW4lker demonstrates why organizations need to look beyond traditional phishing prevention and MFA when evaluating identity security. Three priorities deserve attention:

Close authentication policy gaps. Review where device-code authentication is genuinely required. Restrict or block unnecessary use through Microsoft Entra Conditional Access to reduce opportunities for attackers to abuse legitimate authentication flows.

Strengthen detection across email and identity systems. Ensure the SOC can connect suspicious attachments, phishing infrastructure, and unusual authentication events. Better visibility across these stages helps teams identify potential compromises before attackers expand their access.

Reduce investigation time and escalation costs. Equip Tier 1 analysts with historical threat context and clear escalation criteria. Establish procedures for containing compromised accounts and reviewing unauthorized activity, helping Tier 2 teams focus on incidents requiring deeper investigation.

SkyW4lker continues to evolve, with new endpoints, changing URL patterns, and growing activity across sandbox analyses. Its connection to Gabagool suggests that the same developer is supporting both device-code and credential phishing, giving attackers different ways to compromise business accounts through shared infrastructure.

For organizations, the findings highlight a broader security challenge: attackers are increasingly exploiting legitimate authentication processes and trusted business services, making malicious activity harder to distinguish from normal operations.

As phishing kits evolve, security teams need more than traditional email filtering and MFA. Stronger identity controls, visibility into suspicious authentication activity, and access to connected threat context can help SOCs identify attacks earlier, investigate them faster, and reduce the potential impact on business operations.

#9769. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9767. Reuse a Cached App Shell Without Blurring Query-Driven Responses

Posted on Nov 12 • Originally published at chriseugenerodriguez.com

A cached app shell may fail to load offline when a navigation adds a tracking or cosmetic query parameter. A request for /app and one for /app?utm_source=newsletter are different URLs under default cache matching, even when both should receive the same shell document.

The safe fix is route-scoped rather than global. First classify the request: allow only GET requests for a canonical shell path such as /app. For that one lane, use a cache lookup that ignores the URL search component. The cached shell can then satisfy navigations with campaign tags or other parameters that do not alter the shell response. The request still carries its full URL; only cache comparison changes.

Leave every other request on exact matching. API endpoints, searches, filtered results, user profiles, reports, and locale-specific content often use query parameters to select the response. In those cases, ignoring search could make one request receive a response intended for another query. Non-GET requests should bypass this shell-cache policy and continue to the network.

Expected behavior is intentionally limited. Two shell navigations with harmlessly different query strings can use one cached shell entry. If that entry is absent, the request falls back to the network. A query-sensitive request remains keyed by its complete URL and cannot select another query’s cached response.

Keep the decision function separate from service-worker event wiring. A controlled fixture can verify that application code selects the intended lookup option, preserves exact matching elsewhere, and bypasses non-GET requests. It cannot prove browser Cache API behavior, secure-context requirements, or the service-worker lifecycle; those require browser integration verification.

Ignoring search does not normalize different paths, reorder parameters, or establish a caching strategy for every route. Use it only where the path identifies a reusable shell and the search string does not change what that response means.

#9766. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9765. WCAG 2.2 et RGAA : ce qui change pour votre site

Posted on Nov 12 • Originally published at claren.fr

Les WCAG 2.2, publiées par le W3C le 5 octobre 2023, ajoutent neuf critères de succès et retirent le critère 4.1.1. Le RGAA 4.1.2, toujours en vigueur, vérifie les critères de niveaux A et AA des WCAG 2.1. L’intégration des WCAG 2.2 est annoncée pour le RGAA 5 : une commune audite aujourd’hui sur le RGAA 4.1.2, et peut déjà tenir compte des nouveaux critères dans ses projets.

Ce sont les règles internationales d’accessibilité des contenus web. Elles sont rédigées par un groupe de travail du W3C, le consortium qui publie les standards du web. Leurs critères de succès sont rangés sous quatre principes : perceptible, utilisable, compréhensible, robuste.

Le W3C encourage à utiliser la dernière version. Il précise qu’un contenu conforme aux WCAG 2.2 l’est aussi aux WCAG 2.1 et 2.0.

Chaque critère des WCAG porte un niveau. Une page est conforme au niveau A si elle respecte tous les critères de niveau A. Elle est conforme au niveau AA si elle respecte tous les critères de niveaux A et AA. Le niveau AAA suppose en plus tous les critères AAA.

Le W3C lui-même déconseille d’exiger le niveau AAA pour un site entier. Certains contenus ne peuvent pas satisfaire tous les critères AAA.

« RGAA niveau AA » ou « RGAA AA » désigne donc les niveaux A et AA ensemble. La méthode du RGAA 4.1.2 vérifie les 50 critères de succès de niveaux A et AA des WCAG 2.1 retenus par la norme européenne EN 301 549. Le RGAA ne vérifie pas le niveau AAA. Le détail est dans RGAA : c’est quoi, qui est concerné.

Neuf critères : deux de niveau A, quatre de niveau AA et trois de niveau AAA. Six entrent donc dans le niveau AA. Les intitulés officiels sont en anglais ; la description est la nôtre, résumée du texte du W3C.

Les neuf critères ajoutés par les WCAG 2.2

Pour un site communal, trois de ces critères touchent des parcours fréquents : la taille des boutons et des liens sur mobile, les formulaires en plusieurs étapes, et la connexion à un espace personnel.

Le critère 4.1.1, « Parsing », visait la syntaxe du code HTML. Le W3C explique qu’il répondait à un besoin disparu : les technologies d’assistance n’analysent plus directement le HTML. Les problèmes qu’il couvrait n’existent plus ou relèvent d’autres critères. Il est marqué « obsolète et retiré » dans les WCAG 2.2.

Ce retrait ne vaut pas pour le RGAA 4.1.2. Son critère 8.2 vérifie que le code source est valide, et il renvoie aux critères 4.1.1 et 4.1.2 des WCAG 2.1. Tant que le RGAA 4.1.2 est en vigueur, un audit teste donc toujours ce critère.

Les WCAG 2.2 reprennent les critères des versions 2.0 et 2.1, sauf le 4.1.1. Elles ajoutent les neuf critères du tableau. Un site conforme aux WCAG 2.2 niveau AA est conforme aux WCAG 2.1 niveau AA. L’inverse n’est pas garanti : les six critères AA ajoutés n’ont pas été vérifiés.

Pour la déclaration d’accessibilité d’une commune, la question ne se pose pas encore. Le taux publié est calculé sur les 106 critères du RGAA 4.1.2, selon la méthode officielle de calcul.

Les trois textes avancent l’un après l’autre.

Pour une boutique en ligne, la référence est la norme EN 301 549, pas le RGAA. Le passage aux WCAG 2.2 y dépendra de la citation de la nouvelle version au Journal officiel.

Auditer sur le RGAA 4.1.2, publier ses documents, et préparer la suite sans attendre.

Nos audits suivent la méthode du RGAA 4.1.2. Chaque défaut devient une fiche de correction que le prestataire du site peut reprendre. L’offre est décrite sur la page Prestations.

Non. Le RGAA 4.1.2 vérifie les 50 critères de niveaux A et AA des WCAG 2.1 retenus par la norme EN 301 549. L’intégration des WCAG 2.2 est annoncée pour le RGAA 5.

Neuf : deux de niveau A, quatre de niveau AA et trois de niveau AAA. Le critère 4.1.1 est retiré.

Non. Le RGAA ne vérifie que les niveaux A et AA, et le W3C déconseille d’exiger le niveau AAA pour un site entier.

Pas pour un organisme public. La déclaration d’accessibilité rend compte d’un audit sur les critères du RGAA en vigueur, aujourd’hui le RGAA 4.1.2.

Avec le RGAA 5. La DINUM prévoit sa sortie en décembre 2026 et son officialisation par décret courant 2027.

À lire ensuite : Se former à l’accessibilité numérique : les formations publiques.

#9763. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

Note: This article contains affiliate links, meaning we make a small commission if you buy any premium plan from our link.
