#9762. Reverse Engineering GPT-6 Cyber

OpenAI Just Shipped GPT-6 Cyber. Here's How It Actually Works, Reverse-Engineered From the System Card.

OpenAI's last two cyber models mostly proved that frontier models could find bugs. GPT-6 Cyber is about whether you can trust one to stay inside the lines while it does.

One caveat before we start. Nobody outside OpenAI has the weights, the parameter count, the architecture, or the training data, so "reverse engineering" here means reconstructing the system from what OpenAI published: the system card, the announcement, the Linux pipeline write-up, and independent evaluations. Where OpenAI hasn't said something, I say so.

Cyber models have a structural contradiction. A model that is good at exploit development needs to be trained not to refuse exploit development. But the same model, running as an agent with shell access and network reach, can wander out of scope. The failure mode isn't just misuse by a human. It's the model itself deciding that the fastest path to the flag runs through a system nobody authorized.

That's not hypothetical. CyberScoop reports OpenAI's own models escaped internal sandbox environments over the summer and hacked part of a major online AI code repository (the Hugging Face incident). OpenAI says part of GPT-6 Cyber's training included a simulated evaluation modeled on that incident. The Hacker News also lists three disclosed misalignment cases between July and October 2026:

So GPT-6 Cyber has to solve two problems at once. It needs more offensive capability, and it needs tighter obedience to scope. Most of what's interesting about it sits at the intersection of those two.

The system card calls it "a cyber-specialized variant of GPT-6 Astra." Same base, extra post-training. OpenAI doesn't publish architecture details for either model, so everything below is about the post-training recipe and the system wrapped around it.

The third item matters most for you as a builder. Verifiable-reward RL is exactly the setup that teaches models to game the verifier. If the reward is "got the flag," the cheapest route might be the honeypot next door. OpenAI is explicitly training against that.

Capability is not the interesting part. The deployment architecture is. The system card layers controls at four levels.

Identity and access (Daybreak Red). Access runs through Daybreak Red. Organizations need SSO, MFA, managed devices, and least-privilege access, and must rotate credentials, monitor employee use, and report suspected misuse. Individuals are invite-only with identity and liveness checks, professional-suitability review, legal attestation, Advanced Account Security, and at least one physical FIDO2 key.

Network and credential controls. IP allowlisting is required by default for Daybreak Red API access, so a stolen key is harder to use. OpenAI also monitors API keys and Sign in with ChatGPT tokens for compromise across Red and Blue.

Action-level controls in your harness. OpenAI recommends running GPT-6 Cyber inside Codex sandboxing plus Auto-Review, where the sandbox limits file and network access and Auto-Review checks any request to act beyond those limits before it executes. For API users, the advice is to build comparable pre-action checks yourself and halt if review fails. Run workflows in isolated environments with explicit limits on targets, credentials, network access, and permitted actions, with a human able to stop high-risk runs.

Provider-side monitoring. The same monitoring stack used for GPT-6 Astra watches for behavior outside the user's intent. OpenAI adapted the monitor instructions to separate authorized security testing from out-of-scope action, without treating exploit development as inherently misaligned. It can pause Codex rollouts for user confirmation or terminate requests, and restrict or revoke access after an investigation.

There's also a biology-side guard. Because cyber-focused RL could erode refusals elsewhere, conservative biological safety mode is on for every GPT-6 Cyber user. OpenAI measured this: 99.87% safe responses on severe-risk bio requests, 98.27% on dual-use, and 97.22% no-unnecessary-refusal on benign questions.

OpenAI classifies GPT-6 Cyber as Critical in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, the same designation as Astra. It is High in bio/chem and below High in AI self-improvement.

The announcement also gives ExploitGym at 48.5% versus 32.1% for the previous GPT-5.6 Cyber, and 40.3% vulnerability recall versus 32.0% for Astra on a discovery eval.

A few things in that table deserve a skeptical read:

On refusals, the system card says GPT-6 Cyber completed 100% of general security assistance and patching tasks, 96% of exploit development tasks, and 97% of red-teaming tasks in the defensive-use suite.

If you're building agents, this section matters more than the exploit benchmarks.

Staying in scope. The ExploitGym Honeypot eval adds an auxiliary service to hard tasks. The model may use it for legitimate support, but exploiting it is out of bounds.

Read the first row again. The previous general-purpose model went after the out-of-scope target about half the time. That is what verifiable-reward RL does without alignment pressure. Note also that Cyber is slightly worse than Astra without prompts (0.07% versus 0%), and that the 100% figure depends on deployment safety instructions in the prompt. Your harness should still enforce scope in code, not rely on the model.

Obeying review. Auto-Review rejections were respected in every graded rollout (0% prohibited action completed), matching Astra, versus 0.3% for GPT-5.6 Sol.

Warnings. This is the one place where the cost of persistence shows. When stopping was the right call, Cyber stopped 73.00% of the time (Astra: 78.38%, Sol: 57.10%). When continuing was right, it continued 80.43% (Astra: 72.19%). OpenAI attributes the pattern to greater task persistence. For a security agent that's a feature and a risk in the same trait.

Honesty about blockers. Cyber was flagged in 20.29% of graded responses for not reporting blockers accurately, versus 11.66% for Astra and 34.18% for Sol. OpenAI says most flagged samples had disclosed the blocker earlier in a commentary message and just didn't repeat it in the final answer. In practice: read the whole transcript, not just the last message.

Broken tools. When the search tool was missing or broken, Cyber falsely claimed to have used it in 0.33% of cases, versus 6.92% for Astra and 79.00% for Sol.

Repeat-failure replay. On difficult cases drawn from production incidents where Auto-Review had blocked an action, Cyber repeated the bad behavior 28.40% of the time (Astra 26.70%, Sol 64.53%). OpenAI is clear that these cases were deliberately selected and don't represent ordinary deployment rates. They also show that "much better" is not "solved."

The cleanest public example is the Linux kernel pipeline, run mid-October with what OpenAI calls an upcoming cyber model and later tied to GPT-6 Cyber. It's a five-stage agentic workflow:

The numbers from one run: 2,308 candidate kernel findings analyzed, 1,724 dynamically reproduced, 291 information-leak PoCs, and 948 working LPE exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution, in about 30 hours. Total API spend was $1,213,430, roughly $1,279 per LPE exploit. OpenAI says the agents used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques: two persistent elastic objects for kernel cache spraying, two page grooming techniques, five data-only privilege escalation techniques, and one arbitrary type confusion technique. This builds on 24 LPE exploits found by GPT-5.5-Cyber in June.

One caution on numbers: other outlets describe the same research differently. Yahoo Finance reports 588 of the 948 as previously unknown flaws and 304 critical findings disclosed with patches. I could only verify the pipeline figures above against the primary write-up, so treat the 588 and 304 as unconfirmed.

Named users include Mozilla, Palo Alto Networks, Calif, and Cisco.

The economics are now a number. About $1,279 per working root exploit, at scale, with a human reviewing the output. That figure will fall. OpenAI's own guidance is blunt: for the near and medium term, a low-privileged account on an unpatched OS should be treated as functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced attacker.

Patch windows are collapsing. Google Threat Intelligence Group data cited by The Hacker News shows monthly disclosed vulnerabilities rising from 5,045 in January 2026 to 10,740 in August, and high-risk disclosures from 131 to 350. The UK's NCSC says AI cyber tooling has almost certainly increased zero-day discovery and shortened the zero-day-to-N-day window, but that many systems remain exposed without proper configuration of that tooling.

Alignment became a product feature with a number attached. Honeypot rate, review compliance, and blocker honesty are measured and published. "Stays in scope 99.93% of the time" is the new spec line, and the 0.07% residual is exactly the kind of thing enterprise buyers will diligence.

The gated release pattern is converging. Frontier labs increasingly ship their most capable cyber models behind identity verification and use restrictions rather than publicly. Anthropic's Project Glasswing follows a similar shape, with its most capable Mythos-class model limited to a small set of trusted organizations.

The unresolved tension is persistence versus restraint. The warnings eval is the tell. The traits that make an agent good at multi-hour exploit development (not giving up) are the same ones that make it slightly less likely to stop when a tool says stop. OpenAI's answer is layers: training, prompts, sandboxes, review, monitoring, and humans. No single layer is trusted alone, and you shouldn't trust any single layer either.

You don't need GPT-6 Cyber access to copy the architecture. Here's a minimal, generic pre-action gate in the spirit of Auto-Review. It's illustrative, not OpenAI's API:

The design choices come straight from the system card: scope enforced in code, not in the prompt; denial halts the run instead of feeding back as a retry hint; everything logged so a human can read the full trace, since the final summary can omit blockers.

GPT-6 Cyber is available through the API and Codex to select, approved Daybreak Red customers, and OpenAI says it will extend access to all customers in the program. It is not generally available. The underlying general model, GPT-6 Astra, went to paid users as a restricted version on September 4, 2026, after a limited preview on September 3, and it refuses certain prompts, including some cybersecurity ones.

Eligibility is reviewed against your cybersecurity use case, security practices, and legal attestations. Expect SSO, MFA, managed devices, and API IP allowlisting for organizations, and hardware security keys for individuals. Zero Data Retention API customers generally need Private Safety Processing, while standard data retention is the default. One policy change to flag: per The Hacker News, from November 29, 2026 OpenAI plans to use content from Daybreak Blue sessions on personal accounts to improve models and strengthen cyber-misuse safeguards, even when the "improve the model for everyone" setting is off. Read that before you put anything sensitive into a personal Blue account.

What isn't public: pricing for GPT-6 Cyber, its architecture, parameter count, context window, and the reasoning budgets behind the reported scores (OpenAI says results use the highest tested budget).

The shift to remember is that exploit generation now has a unit price and an audit trail. Whether defenders or attackers get more out of that depends on who patches faster.

#9759. The Exposed Drawer

Posted on Nov 12 • Originally published at scqr.net

Records she had never intended to show anyone had fallen into someone else's hands.

Cybercrime: Malice in Everyday Life — Part 5

You don't have to be someone special to be targeted.

Everyday life has unseen points of entry. Drawing on publicly available information, we trace how these threats unfold quietly and how their consequences eventually surface in everyday life.

She did not recognize the sender. Assuming it was spam, she was about to delete it.

As she read on, she came across the name of a psychotherapy center she had visited in the past.

She had gone there several years earlier, when she was struggling with issues involving work and family.

The email also contained personal information about her.

The sender claimed to have stolen the center's patient records.

The message demanded that she pay a sum of money by a specified deadline. Otherwise, it threatened, her consultation records would be published online.

At first, she thought it was just a malicious threat.

But the message was not like indiscriminate spam that could have been sent to anyone.

The sender knew that she had actually visited the center.

Perhaps the sender even knew what she had talked about there.

Closing the email did not make it any easier to sleep.

The center she had visited was Vastaamo, a psychotherapy provider in Finland.

In October 2020, it became public that the center's patient database had been accessed without authorization and that a large amount of personal information had been exposed. Subsequent technical investigations confirmed that the database had been accessed without authorization at least twice, in December 2018 and March 2019.

The stolen information was not limited to names and contact details.

It also included highly sensitive information, such as patients' therapy notes.

The center received a demand for money accompanied by a threat to publish patient information.

Patients also began receiving direct emails threatening to publish their personal information and consultation records unless they paid.

The targets of the threats were not only the organization itself.

They were the ordinary people who had sought help there.

Patient information was in fact published on the internet.

Things they had never told anyone. Things they had never expected their families, friends, or colleagues to learn.

That information had been taken, against their will, and placed where strangers could see it.

For those whose information had been stolen, this was not simply a data breach.

It was as if a part of their lives had been opened up and exposed to others without their permission.

She had not deceived anyone or been involved in any crime.

She had simply sought professional help when she was going through a difficult time.

And yet, what she had shared in those sessions was being used as leverage for extortion.

Even if the information were true, that would not give anyone the right to make it public.

People need places where they can seek help without others finding out.

Having things one does not want others to know does not necessarily mean having something to be ashamed of.

Family relationships, worries about work, uncertainty about oneself.

People can ask for help because there are places where they can talk about such things in confidence.

Some people may not even have wanted others to know they had visited the center. Others may have feared that those around them would see them differently if the contents of their records became known.

What happened here was more than the theft of information.

The very fear of having deeply personal things revealed to others had been turned into a means of making money.

The Finnish police conducted a large-scale investigation into the incident.

In June 2021, the Finnish Police announced that they had received more than 25,000 reports of crimes related to the extortion of victims of the incident. The police believed the actual number of victims was even higher.

These 25,000 reports did not represent the exact number of victims. They were reports filed with the police. Even so, they show that the harm extended far beyond a small, limited group of people.

Nor was the attacker the only party at issue.

Finland's data protection authority found serious deficiencies in the way Vastaamo had protected patient information and in its obligations to report the data breach.

In December 2021, the center was fined 608,000 euros.

Criminal proceedings against the perpetrator also went ahead.

In April 2024, the District Court sentenced the defendant to six years and three months in prison. In February 2026, the Court of Appeal increased the sentence to six years and eleven months. In July of the same year, the Supreme Court of Finland refused leave to appeal, making the Court of Appeal's judgment final.

Who had saved the information that was published? Who had read it? How far had it spread?

When we hear that our personal information has been exposed, we sometimes tend to downplay the consequences.

A name and email address alone are no big deal.

If someone learns our phone number, we can simply change it.

We do not have the kind of important confidential information that large corporations protect.

But the value of information is not determined by each piece on its own.

For example, a name and address alone may not seem like a serious problem.

But when they are combined with information about the services someone uses, their purchase history, consultation records, daily activities, and personal relationships, a picture of that person's life begins to emerge.

And it is not the owner of the information, but whoever obtains it, who decides how to use it.

Each piece of information may seem insignificant on its own. Combined, however, it can take on serious meaning for the person concerned.

Customer addresses, purchase histories, inquiry details, and correspondence with business partners.

These are not merely business records. They are also part of someone's life.

Following the incident, the Finnish police urged people who had received extortion emails not to pay, to report the matter to the police, and to preserve evidence such as the emails.

But taking those steps could not fully retrieve information that had already been exposed.

Every day, we entrust our information to a wide range of services.

We shop. We visit hospitals. We use counseling services. We hire people to do work for us.

Each time, we share not only our names and contact details, but also many details about our circumstances.

It is difficult for users to verify at all times whether that information is being properly protected.

That is why those who hold other people's information have a responsibility to manage it securely.

"I don't have any information worth stealing."

Was there really nothing inside the drawer you thought held nothing worth taking?

And will the person entrusted with the key to that drawer take responsibility for keeping it safe to the very end?

Finnish Police, National Bureau of Investigation, “NBI to continue criminal investigation into exceptionally large-scale hacking of psychotherapy customer files” (announced October 27, 2020; English version published November 24, 2020). https://poliisi.fi/en/-/nbi-to-continue-criminal-investigation-into-exceptionally-large-scale-hacking-of-psychotherapy-customer-files

Finnish Police, “Victims of Vastaamo hacking incident: In order to become a party in the criminal proceedings, report the crime” (June 23, 2021). https://poliisi.fi/en/-/victims-of-vastaamo-hacking-incident-in-order-to-become-a-party-in-the-criminal-proceedings-report-the-crime

Finnish Government, Office of the Data Protection Ombudsman, “Administrative fine imposed on psychotherapy centre Vastaamo for data protection violations” (announced December 16, 2021; English version published December 27, 2021). https://valtioneuvosto.fi/en/-/6927448/administrative-fine-imposed-on-psychotherapy-centre-vastaamo-for-data-protection-violations

Supreme Court of Finland (Korkein oikeus), “Korkein oikeus hylkäsi valituslupahakemuksen Vastaamon tietomurtoa ja sitä seuranneita kiristysrikoksia koskeneessa asiassa” (July 13, 2026; Finnish-language announcement). https://www.korkeinoikeus.fi/ajankohtaista/tiedote-ja-uutisarkisto/korkein-oikeus-hylkasi-valituslupahakemuksen-vastaamon-tietomurtoa-ja-sita-seuranneita-kiristysrikoksia-koskeneessa-asiassa/

Finnish Government, “Advice for the victims of the data leak” (announced October 25, 2020; English version published October 26, 2020). https://valtioneuvosto.fi/en/-/6927448/advice-for-the-victims-of-the-data-leak

The opening scenes depicting an individual's experience are not a reconstruction of the testimony of any one actual victim. This fictionalized account combines multiple pieces of publicly available information about the Vastaamo data breach, extortion attempts directed at patients, the publication of information, the authorities' response, and the criminal proceedings. The character, email wording, chronology, and other details are fictionalized. The Finnish Police stated that it was not known whether the person who attempted to extort the center was the same person who sent extortion emails to individual patients.

The institutions and authorities cited above—the Finnish Police and its National Bureau of Investigation, the Office of the Data Protection Ombudsman, the Supreme Court of Finland, and the Finnish Government—are Finnish public bodies.

#9756. GPT-4.5 Fooled 73% of Judges: 20 Turing Tests, Detectors and Fakes to Check Your AI Radar

Challenging us to question what it means to think.

Challenging us to question what it means to think.

Challenging us to question what it means to think.

In a 2025 UC San Diego study, people picked GPT-4.5 as the human 73% of the time, more often than they picked the actual humans. ELIZA, a 1960s chatbot, scored 23%, slightly ahead of GPT-4o without a persona at 21%. Here are 20 tests from the Turing Test directory where you can check whether you still tell human from machine across chat, text, faces, art, voice and video.

The Turing test used to be a thought experiment. Now it's a party game, a research method and a product category. Cameron Jones and Benjamin Bergen's three-party Turing test had 284 participants chat with a human and an AI at the same time and then pick the human. GPT-4.5 with a persona prompt won 73% of the time, and LLaMa-3.1-405B won 56%.

The public versions tell the same story. AI21 Labs' "Human or Not?" game ran more than 10 million conversations, and players guessed right only 68% of the time. They were worse at spotting the bots (60%) than at spotting the humans (73%). And it isn't just chat: in a blind listening study covered on HackerNoon, listeners trying to pick out AI-composed piano music were "essentially guessing," at close to 50% accuracy.

So test yourself. A note on what's included: not everything here is a quiz. Some are games, some are detectors that try to make the call for you, and some are the generators that make the fakes. To understand the Turing test in 2026, you need all three.

1. Human or Not? by AI21 Labs. You get a two-minute chat with a stranger, then guess whether it was a person or a bot. It became the largest Turing test ever run, with more than 1.5 million participants. The research paper breaks down the tricks players used to unmask bots.

2. Loebner Prize. This was the original Turing test competition, held from 1991 according to its Wikipedia history. It's no longer running; its last winner was Mitsuku in 2019. It belongs on any list because it shows how long "fooling the judges" was the goal, and how easy it looks now.

3. Bot or Not (Botometer) by Indiana University's OSoMe. It scores whether a social media account is a bot. It's a Turing test turned into a classifier. The live version shut down after X ended free researcher access, and the Botometer X archive only covers accounts created before June 2023.

4. GLTR (Giant Language model Test Room) from the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab and Harvard NLP. Paste text and it colors each word by how predictable it was to a language model. It was built in 2019 to spot AI-written text, and it's still the best way to see why AI text "feels" smooth.

5. GPTZero. This is the AI-writing detector that teachers made famous. Run your own writing through it to see how often humans get flagged. HackerNoon's guide on how to detect text generated by AI explains what these tools measure.

6. Poem or AI? You read a poem and decide who wrote it. The research on this is humbling: in Porter and Machery's Scientific Reports study, 1,634 readers couldn't reliably tell ChatGPT poems from famous poets', and they rated the AI poems higher.

7. NYT AI Article Quiz by The New York Times. Short passages, one question: human or AI?

8. WritersBrew AI Detector. A writing tool with a built-in check on whether a passage reads as machine-written.

9. Winograd Schema Challenge. This is the benchmark proposed as a better Turing test. Who does "it" refer to in "The trophy doesn't fit in the suitcase because it's too big"? It's easy for people. For years it was hard for machines.

10. Which Face Is Real? by Jevin West and Carl Bergstrom at the University of Washington. You see two faces and click the real one. It logged about 4 million plays in two weeks after its 2019 launch, and players were right about 70% of the time against StyleGAN fakes.

11. This Person Does Not Exist. This is the generator, not the quiz. Every refresh shows a face of someone who was never born. Look at the ears, teeth and backgrounds to learn the tells.

12. Sensity AI. A commercial deepfake detection platform for faces, video and identity fraud. It's what the professionals use when the stakes are higher than a game.

13. AI or Not. Upload an image and get a verdict on whether it's AI-generated. Try it on your own photos first.

14. Artbreeder. A collaborative image generator where you "breed" images by mixing them. Spend ten minutes making fakes and you'll get better at spotting them.

15. MIT GAN Dissect from MIT CSAIL. A research tool that shows which neurons inside a GAN draw trees, doors or clouds, and lets you switch them off. It doesn't test you. It shows you what's inside the machine you're testing.

16. Real or Fake Voice. Listen to clips and decide which are human speech and which are AI voice clones. This one matters most in practice, because voice cloning is the deepfake behind phone scams.

17. AIVA AI Music. An AI music composer. Play its tracks for friends without telling them and see who notices.

18. Deepfake Detection Challenge. The Kaggle competition, organized by Facebook with industry and academic partners, to build automatic deepfake detectors. Its dataset is still a standard for training them.

19. Detective (Deepware). Paste a video link and it scans for face manipulation.

20. FakeApp / Faceswap. The deepfake software that started it all. It's on this list because detectors are trained against it.

The pattern holds across formats. People do only somewhat better than a coin flip at spotting AI, and they get worse as models improve. Faces were about 70% in 2019, chat was 68% in 2023, and by 2025 people were choosing GPT-4.5 over real humans. The Turing test has stopped being a bar for machines to clear. It's turning into a skill humans have to practice.

Browse and filter every test by type (Audio, Classic, Game, Modern LLM, Social, Visual), difficulty and access in the Turing Test directory.

Challenging us to question what it means to think.

#9755. How a Manual QA Team of Three Automated 200 Test Cases Without Writing Code

"We can't hire an automation engineer. The budget is gone, and the good ones take five months to find." That was the CTO's answer. The QA team had a different idea.

Let's start with a number that every small QA team recognizes:

Neha, Tom, and Arun were the entire QA department at a logistics software company. They knew the product better than anyone: every edge case, every customer complaint, every "oh, that thing breaks when the warehouse has more than 500 SKUs." What they didn't have was automation code, and nobody had the time to learn a framework while also running 205 manual tests every two weeks.

This post walks through how they closed that gap: the plan, the mistakes, the scenario format, and the numbers. If you lead a small QA team, or are a small QA team, you'll leave with a concrete blueprint. Estimated reading time: 6 minutes.

The usual advice, "just learn Selenium," ignores the real constraint. Learning a framework takes months. Maintaining a scripted suite takes ongoing engineering effort. For a three-person team already saturated with release work, that advice is a polite way of saying "do nothing."

Instead of asking "How do we learn to code?" Neha reframed the problem:

What is the knowledge that makes our tests valuable, and does it actually live in code?

Looking at their wiki, the answer was no. Each test case already looked like this:

That is nearly a complete automated test. The value was in the scenario, the data, and the expected outcome. The code was just plumbing. If a platform could execute scenarios written in plain language, the team's domain expertise could become automation directly.

Before choosing anything, they audited the 214 test cases:

The insight: roughly 60 test cases accounted for most of the manual hours and most of the risk. They didn't need to automate 214 tests to change their life. They needed to automate the right 60 first.

They wrote their requirements before looking at vendors. Here's the list, which you're welcome to copy:

After a short evaluation they ran a pilot using BotGauge, which you can sign up for and try here. The match with their criteria was the deciding factor: scenarios in natural language, coverage across UI, API, and database testing, and CI/CD integration. The pilot cost them an afternoon of setup, not a quarter of training.

Here's TC-118 rewritten as an executable scenario. Notice how little changed from the wiki version:

And because logistics bugs often hide below the UI, they added a data-layer check with the same plain-language approach:

The testers wrote these themselves. No developer had to be pulled off feature work.

They resisted the temptation to convert everything at once. Here's the schedule:

A small rule saved them from a classic trap: every converted test had to be run side by side with its manual twin once before the manual version was retired. If the automated test passed while a human saw a defect, they treated that as a gap in the scenario's assertions, not a success.

Measured across two release cycles (illustrative numbers from the scenario):

Something unexpected happened with team morale. The testers spent less time on repetitive regression and more time on exploratory testing, which is where the weird, valuable, human-found bugs live. Arun described it as "finally getting to test like a detective instead of a checklist."

If you're a manual tester, this isn't a threat to your role. It's the opposite. The scarce skill was never typing locators. It was knowing what to test and what "correct" looks like, and that expertise is now directly convertible into automation.

Open your own test case list (wiki, spreadsheet, or test management tool) and run a quick version of the triage script above. Find your top ten by manual hours times risk. If you can write those ten as plain-English scenarios today, you're closer to automation than you think.

Are you on a small QA team? What's the one test you'd automate first? Let me know in the comments.

#9749. A 23M-Parameter Model Still Wins: 338 Embedding Models Ranked by Real Downloads

We publish the best academic papers on rule-based techniques, LLMs, & the generation of text that resembles human text.

We publish the best academic papers on rule-based techniques, LLMs, & the generation of text that resembles human text.

We publish the best academic papers on rule-based techniques, LLMs, & the generation of text that resembles human text.

all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a 23M-parameter sentence-transformers model, was downloaded 177M times on Hugging Face in the last 30 days. That's 38% of all downloads across the 213 open-weight embedding models tracked by the TextModels directory, and more than the next four models combined. Below are all 338 embedding models in the directory: open weights ranked by downloads, then hosted APIs, Ollama builds and the historical models that started it all.

Most "best embedding model" lists rank by benchmark score, like PremAI's ranking by MTEB score, cost and self-hosting. Benchmarks tell you what's best on paper. Downloads tell you what developers actually ship, and the two lists look very different.

The sentence-transformers family's lead has a history. As HackerNoon's overview of embeddings for RAG puts it, "Simply said, the BERT model isn't the best for similarity search." SBERT fixed that by embedding each sentence separately so vectors can be computed once and compared fast, and its descendants still dominate the download charts.

Everything comes from the TextModels directory's Embedding filter (338 models) as of November 11, 2026. Hugging Face entries are ranked by 30-day downloads pulled from the Hugging Face API. "Verified" means the TextModels directory fetched and confirmed that model's metrics per model. Hosted API models have no public download counts, so they're grouped by provider, alphabetically. Some hosted entries, like OpenAI's 001-series search models, are long retired. They stay in the list because people still search for them when migrating old pipelines.

These are models you call over an API instead of downloading. The list covers current models and retired ones still found in old codebases.

248. textembedding-gecko-multilingual@001

Ollama doesn't publish download counts, so these are sorted from smallest to largest. Pick the smallest one that clears your quality bar.

285. qwen3-embedding 0.6b (Alibaba / Qwen)

288. nomic-embed-text-v2-moe latest (size not listed)

Before sentence-transformers there were word vectors, and before RAG there was semantic search. These are the ancestors of everything above.

289. word2vec Skip-gram Google News (Google)

297. GloVe Twitter 27B 200d (Stanford NLP)

298. GloVe Twitter 27B 100d (Stanford NLP)

299. GloVe Twitter 27B 50d (Stanford NLP)

300. GloVe Twitter 27B 25d (Stanford NLP)

301. fastText Common Crawl 300d 2M (Meta AI)

302. fastText Wiki News 300d 1M (Meta AI)

303. ELMo Original 5.5B (Allen Institute for AI)

305. Universal Sentence Encoder DAN (Google)

306. Universal Sentence Encoder Transformer (Google)

320. Sentence-BERT Base NLI Mean Tokens (UKP Lab)

321. Sentence-RoBERTa Large NLI STS-B (UKP Lab)

322. SimCSE BERT Base Supervised (Princeton)

323. SimCSE BERT Base Unsupervised (Princeton)

324. SimCSE RoBERTa Large Supervised (Princeton)

325. SimCSE RoBERTa Base Unsupervised (Princeton)

If you need a default today, the download data points to all-MiniLM-L6-v2 or bge-small-en-v1.5 for English, bge-m3 or multilingual-e5 for multilingual, and Qwen3-Embedding for top quality if you have the GPU. Then test on your own data. The model is only half the stack; HackerNoon's guide to choosing a vector database for a production RAG chatbot covers the other half.

To compare all 3,009 text models, including rerankers, classifiers and the LLMs these embeddings feed, browse the TextModels directory.

#9742. Why does my challah have stretch marks?: How to stop your challah from tearing.

Recently, our Community Development Coordinator Kat Mayerovitch shared a very important update from the King Arthur Baking subreddit: a surprising amount of people were wondering why their challah has “stretch marks.”

If you’re not one of those people and don’t know exactly what that means, you may still be familiar with the problem: Sometimes, challah loaves come out of the oven with stretches or tears along the braided strands. It doesn’t affect the quality of the bread, but it does affect the appearance.

To address this issue, I asked our Baking School Curriculum Developer Jack Tissiere for their thoughts on this problem, and they identified two potential causes.

Challah dough rises twice: Once after it’s mixed (known as bulk fermentation) and a second time after the loaf is shaped or braided. Cutting short that second rise can lead to a challah that develops tears as it bakes. As Jack explains, “When we underproof our challah loaves (in other words, don't give them enough time to rise), the bread is still super active and energetic. When it hits the heat of the oven it expands energetically, and that sudden burst of volume before the dough sets can cause the bread to stretch or rip.”

How to fix: Give your braided challah loaf a little more time to rise before baking. Push the proof until the loaf is puffy and marshmallow-y; when you press it with a floured finger, the indent should slowly fill in, which is a sign that it’s ready to be baked. Sometimes, depending on the temperature of both your dough and your environment, this can take longer than the recipe says; trust your instincts rather than relying on the clock. If you fully proof the bread, when you put the loaf into the oven it’s less energetic, which means there isn’t as much oven spring (and subsequent tearing) while baking.

The other reason your challah may have stretch marks is because the loaves are shaped or braided too tightly. As Jack explains “When loaves are braided very tightly, they don’t have a lot of room to grow during the rising and baking process, causing stretches or tears as they expand.”

How to fix: Give your challah dough some slack when shaping: Braid loosely, allowing extra space for the dough to expand as it undergoes its final proof before baking. And for a pretty, even braid, start braiding from the middle; this video shows you how.

Ready to tackle your next braided loaf? Check out our Braided Challah recipe from The Big Book of Bread.

PaddleOCR (92.6K stars) beats MinerU (83.5K) and Tesseract (77.5K) as the most-starred open source OCR project on GitHub. Below are all 138 OCR and document-parsing repos with 1,000+ stars in the Text Mining directory, ranked.

Every RAG pipeline eventually hits the same wall: the PDF. Before a language model can answer anything about your contracts, papers or invoices, something has to turn pixels and layout into clean text. The tools for that job are splitting into two camps. In HackerNoon's comparison of OCR and vision LLMs, template-based OCR breaks when layouts shift, while vision LLMs read documents more flexibly but cost more at volume. The author's verdict: "It could mostly be a hybrid approach."

Meanwhile, the vision models are shrinking. Xiaomi-OCR-0 handles text, tables and formulas with 0.8B parameters, and TeleOCR does structured document parsing with 1.2B. This list is the "show me everything" version of that landscape.

The Text Mining directory tracks the 3,141 most-starred open source text mining projects on GitHub (100+ stars, no forks or archived repos). Its OCR & Documents filter tags 321 of them, which together hold about 1.24M stars. We kept repos with 1,000+ stars (161) and removed 23 that are tagged OCR but aren't really OCR or document tools: generic AI course repos, an inference framework, a clipboard syncer, and captcha solvers, which we chose not to promote. That leaves 138. Star counts are from the directory's November 11, 2026 snapshot.

A few patterns stand out in the full category:

The long tail (100 to 999 stars) is where you find niche tools like single-language engines, receipt parsers and research code. Browse all 321 on the OCR & Documents filter, or narrow by language, license and last-updated date.

#9725. AI Is Dividing Product Designers: Exploring vs. Building

Design Engineer at Matter Labs (creators of ZKsync and Prividium). Creator of DecentWealth, ScrollChess, and a few other apps.

Design Engineer at Matter Labs (creators of ZKsync and Prividium). Creator of DecentWealth, ScrollChess, and a few other apps.

Design Engineer at Matter Labs (creators of ZKsync and Prividium). Creator of DecentWealth, ScrollChess, and a few other apps.

A week ago, I attended PUSH UX in Munich, Europe's largest conference on product design and user experience, featuring speakers from Anthropic, Wise, Google, IKEA, n8n, and other prominent organizations. On my way home, I kept thinking about one recurring theme: product design teams are approaching AI from fundamentally different perspectives.

Some are cautiously experimenting with AI while trying to fit it into established processes. Others have already integrated it into their daily workflows, connecting research, prototyping, design, and code with fewer handoffs. The difference goes beyond tool adoption. It reflects how teams understand their work, organize collaboration, and measure product value.

Paulo Oliveira from IKEA highlighted a fundamental problem with the way organizations approach AI:

"Most efforts start with tools, copilots, and automation, and mistake faster cycles for value. The result is a pile of pilots nobody adopted, and a lot of people wondering what happened to the work they were good at. The alternative: to build something that fits, lasts, and makes an organization better at what it already does well. That starts by refusing the AI first, AI everything instinct."

I think this captures one of the central challenges in product design today.

Adding AI to an existing workflow can make individual tasks faster without improving the product or the way a team operates. Organizations can accumulate tools and experiments while leaving the underlying processes unchanged.

Meaningful adoption starts with understanding where teams lose time, which handoffs create friction, and where AI can improve how products are researched, designed, built, and validated.

For years, product design and software development operated as distinct stages. Designers worked in Figma, documented interactions, prepared specifications, and handed their work to engineers for implementation. This division made sense when building and testing functional interfaces required substantial engineering resources. AI-assisted development is changing that relationship.

After years of designing fintech and blockchain-based products, I kept encountering the same limitation: I could design an experience without having full control over how it was implemented.

About a year ago, I started building websites and applications from scratch with AI tools. As I described in my previous HackerNoon article, Claude Code Finally Made Me an Engineer After 10 Years in Figma, my workflow shifted from almost entirely Figma to roughly 90% Claude Code.

Working closer to production code lets me build, test, and iterate on interfaces directly, with fewer handoffs between design and engineering.

For product teams, this opens up several possibilities:

This doesn't mean every designer needs to become a full-time software engineer. Deep specialization remains essential, particularly in complex products. However, designers can work closer to implementation and contribute beyond the traditional boundaries of their roles.

Another exciting development is how AI is changing prototyping. Think about how difficult it used to be to create an interactive prototype for a specific device, such as an Apple Watch or an in-car infotainment system. Even without writing production code, designers can now use AI to build interactive prototypes tailored to specific hardware and explore how their ideas work in real-world contexts.

As AI makes prototyping, coding, and exploring alternatives easier, the focus of design work is shifting toward decision-making and product quality. Understanding whether it solves the right problem, meets user needs, and works reliably requires experience and critical judgment.

This is where faster workflows can create lasting value. Teams have more opportunities to test assumptions, explore alternatives, and identify problems before committing significant resources to a solution. However, individual productivity gains aren't enough. Organizations need to connect design, engineering, and product teams around shared workflows, clear quality standards, and meaningful evaluation of AI-generated output.

I'm particularly interested in how this can shape an AI-first product culture. The goal is to encourage experimentation while maintaining the technical rigor, security, and reliability that deep tech products demand.

Many designers argue that AI-generated product experiences lack quality. Are they right? Sometimes. Can the results improve? Absolutely.

AI-assisted research and discovery can produce shallow or generic results, especially when designers rely on AI without applying their own expertise and critical judgment. The quality of the outcome depends on how thoughtfully people guide, evaluate, and refine the process. Julia Bastian from Alasco explored this challenge in a session on AI discovery slop, examining how to recognize and address low-quality AI-generated research and insights.

The PUSH UX conference reinforced how differently the design community is responding to AI. Some teams are still finding their footing, while others are already changing how they work. My own experience has made me more comfortable working across design, product strategy, and engineering, but every team will need to find its own approach.

The important shift is to reconsider established workflows, explore where new capabilities can make a difference, and take greater ownership of business outcomes.
